CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue the ongoing negotiations through to the March 1 deadline, match the US's constructive tone, and keep delivering on the promised purchase commitments (soybeans, energy, manufactured goods) as tangible de-escalation currency — but hold firm against US demands for a direct enforcement mechanism that would let Washington monitor Chinese legal and economic decisions, which we must treat as a sovereignty red line. Do not retaliate or escalate further, since that would all but guarantee the $200B tariff tranche jumps from 10% to 25% on March 1 and deepen the damage to an already-slowing export economy.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is real and high, but not existential. US Section 301 tariffs already cover ~$250B of Chinese goods (timeline 2018-09-24), and the suspended Jan 1 hike to 25% on ~$200B is now a hard March 1 deadline (Lighthizer: 'hard deadline'; 2018-12-10/2019-02-14 reporting). This is a genuine overhang on our export base at a moment when China's economy hit a three-decade-low 6.6% growth in 2018 with Q4 at 6.4%, exports contracting in December, and imports from the US down 41.2% — all PIT-visible before the decision date. Huawei is under direct firm-level targeting: DOJ unsealed charges and a formal extradition request on Jan 28 (timeline), and Washington is pressuring allies to exclude Huawei from 5G, a direct assault on our tech-autonomy ambitions (Made in China 2025). That combination — tariff overhang plus tech containment plus a slowing economy — pushes threat to +0.45. It is NOT +0.8/+1.0 because the escalation has been paused: the US suspended the Jan 1 hike, high-level talks are progressing (Jan 30, Feb 14-15) with genuine purchase progress, and both sides have signaled a deal is possible, so this reads as a high, manageable threat rather than an existential one. Actionally, escalatory retaliation is the wrong instrument — it answers the opponent's likely response poorly (raising tariffs to 25% that they have explicitly threatened) and hurts our own slowing exporters; maximal concession is equally wrong because the US demands (IP, forced tech-transfer rollback, subsidy wind-down, and above all an enforcement mechanism) touch core economic sovereignty and would be politically untenable and strategically self-defeating to grant wholesale. The disciplined middle is negotiate: keep the deal alive, bank goodwill through purchases, and probe for an enforcement compromise without pre-committing beyond what talks warrant.
key_factors: US tariffs on ~$250B of Chinese goods at 10%, with $200B tranche set to rise to 25% on March 1 if no deal (hard deadline)
90-day truce from G20 with talks resuming Jan 7, Jan 30, Feb 14-15; progress on purchases, enforcement/structural IP unresolved
Huawei targeted: DOJ charges + extradition request Jan 28; US pressuring allies to bar Huawei from 5G — tech containment of Made in China 2025
China economy at 3-decade low (6.6% in 2018, 6.4% Q4), December export contraction, imports from US down 41.2%; stimulus being deployed
US enforcement-mechanism demand conflicts with China's economic-sovereignty red line
Escalation paused (Jan 1 hike suspended) and both sides signaling a deal is reachable — high but not existential threat
